newsitem.title: CROATIA: Albright scolds Croatia over refugees, war crimes.
newsitem.headline: Albright scolds Croatia over refugees, war crimes.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright scolded Croatia on Saturday for its failure to meet pledges on refugees and war crimes and warned if it did not exercise "moral" leadership in the region Washington would continue to oppose aid and other benefits.
It was the latest in a series of dressings down Washington has given to Croatia and comes just two weeks before Croatian President Franjo Tujdman stands for re-election.
A grim-faced Tudjman took the unusual step of interrupting Albright at a news conference to defend Zagreb's actions, but Albright made clear that keen disagreements remained.

"I believe it is the appropriate role of leadership of every country to provide moral direction...and I asked President Tudjman to provide that kind of leadership," Albright told a joint news conference with Tudjman.

Albright met Foreign Minister Mate Granic in Washington two weeks ago and made it plain the United States expects higher standards from Croatia if it is to achieve its goal of further integration with the West.

She told Tudjman he had to prevent violence against Serb refugees trying to return to pre-war homes in Croatia, and cooperate with the international war crimes tribunal in The Hague, dismissing his statement that recent attacks had been provoked and Zagreb was not capable of preventing them.
U.S. officials described the meeting as frank and said it was the toughest Albright has had with any leader since becoming America's top diplomat in January.

Albright told the Croatian president if he failed to act on the demands, which include commitments he made when signing the 1995 Dayton peace accord that ended the war in Bosnia, the United States would consider blocking International Monetary Fund loans and Croatia's integration into Western institutions.
A U.S. official said later Albright told Tudjman she would personally approve how the United States voted at the IMF.
Her spokesman told reporters the only commitment Tudjman made was to open a bridge at Brcko, over the Sava River from the Bosnian Serb republic to Croatia, to open a trade route.
Tudjman insisted Zagreb supported the right of Serbs to return to their homes and was complying with other aspects of the Dayton accord.

"For all practical purposes Croatia is not embarking on any policy of ethnic purity but rather recognises fully all human and ethnic rights of all communities living in this country, including Serbs...It is now our challenge to create as soon as possible the conditions for co-existance," Tudjman said.

He stressed that thousands of Serbs had returned home in an organised fashion with no reprisals, but Albright told reporters she disagreed with him. "We want to make sure there is freedom of movement. We want to make sure Croatian Serbs who want to return home are free to do so."

Albright left Zagreb to visit a village in the Krajina region where she will meet Serbs who were recently attacked after returning to pre-war homes. The sudden outbreak of violence focused attention on government plans to resettle tens of thousands of displaced people.
Zagreb claims the violence was provoked by the spontaneous and unannounced arrival of Serbs in several villages, but the United States claims local government officials were involved.

Albright told Tudjman it was morally unacceptable to have an ethnically pure state in modern-day Europe. "Croatia will not travel the road to Europe unless all its peoples, Croats or Serbs, make the journey," she told the news conference.

The first issue Albright raised with the Croatian government delegation was that of war criminals. She later took Tudjman aside to ask him where indictee Dario Kordic is -- he is believed to be in Bosnian Croat territory though there are rumours in Zagreb he has fled to South America.
Albright told Tudjman he had to use his influence in the Croat part of Bosnia to hand over war criminals hiding there.

"The Croatian government directly, and by bringing its influence to bear on the Croats of Bosnia-Hercegovina, is doing everything to provide for the full implementation of the Dayton accord," Tudjman replied.
